paper_title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with \texttt{grep}. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over $91$ repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Coding agents are tested on ever newer repository tasks (Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026), but an end-to-end score does not say whether search, reasoning or editing failed. Retrieval benchmarks test search alone. On them, code-specialized encoders beat BM25 by wide nDCG@10 margins (Kryvosheieva et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Yet one practitioner report found that embeddings were not the bottleneck for SWE-bench agent that searched with grep and find (Chen and Flaherty, 2025). Teams build embedding indexes because of bench- *Work done at Ant Group. 1 mark gaps, so the conflict matters. What does the dense advantage buy, and where does it come from? Existing evidence cannot settle this. Embedding benchmarks mostly pair curated or docstring-style queries with old code (Husain et al., 2019; Muennighoff et al., 2023); agent reports use raw issue or pull-request (PR) text (Jimenez et al., 2024). Lexical baselines often reuse the dense retrievers chunking. Weak baselines are known source of false gains in neural ranking (Lin, 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Kamphuis et al., 2020), but their effect in repository code search has not been measured. Gold labels also differ. SWE-benchs gold patches contain no test files (Jimenez et al., 2024). PRs list of changed files does, and those tests count as relevant unless they are removed. Our own first version kept them. Tests can be fair targets elsewhere, so we report both label rules. Finally, benchmark code predates the encoders training cutoffs, so the advantage could also reflect contamination (Magar and Schwartz, 2022; Sainz et al., 2023). To answer this, we build REPOPREMIUM, realistic repository-level code-search benchmark over real repositories with file-level labels. Repository localization pipelines rank files first, and file labels come straight from the merged change (Section 3). Within each repository we fix the code snapshot, the label rule and the protocol, and vary only where the query comes from and when the change was made. The core has 1,265 queries over ten SWE-bench Verified repositories: curated problem statements (OpenAI, 2024) and raw GitHub PR text from 2022, 2023 and 2026.1 Each main analysis is thus repeated across query sources and years. An extension set adds five languages, nine heldout repositories and 91-repository preregistered 1Each raw pool takes PRs merged in one window: 2022 (RAW-PRE22), 2023 (RAW-PRE23) and on or after 2026-0101 (RAW-POST). We skip 20242025 so that every window lies clearly before or after the encoders training cutoffs; see Step 2 of Section 3.2, Table 1 and Section B.1. (Figure 1, Section 5.1). Against whole-file BM25 the encoder still leads the raw pools, mostly through Recall@10; on curated queries its interval covers zero. F2 Adding the codes words closes what remains. The premium sits on queries that lack the codes rare words, and LLM-written identifiers help BM25 far more than the encoder. From the same expanded query the encoder gains fraction of what BM25 gains, and prose stripped of identifiers changes nothing. BM25 then matches or beats dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on PRs newer than the LLM. The LLM may know the repository, so this replaces the premium but does not explain it (Sections 5.2 and 5.4). F3 The two retrievers win different queries, and nothing we tried predicts which. Classifiers, LLM judges and preregistered router all fail. fixed fusion of the two beats either retriever alone and held on 539 preregistered lockbox queries (Sections 5.3 and 5.6). From these findings we derive three guidelines for code search: G1 Measure dense gains against fair lexical baseline. Index whole files for BM25, strip templated PR text, and state which edited files count as relevant before comparing against dense retrieval. G2 Keep dense retrieval and fuse it with BM25. fixed rank fusion beats dense alone on development data and on 539 lockbox queries, and no router beat the fusion. In agents, the LLM matters more than the search tool (Section 5.7). G3 When query names no code, add the codes words before searching. One LLM call that drafts the missing identifiers lets whole-file BM25 match an embedding index. The call recurs per query, so it suits repositories searched rarely (Section E).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent suites such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) and DeepSWE (Huang et al., 2026) run the whole agent loop. Code-retrieval benchmarks such as CoIR (Li et al., 2025) pair docstringor web-style queries with old code. None of them varies query mining and training-cutoff date together. Their labels also differ: SWE-bench gold patches contain no tests, while PRs file list keeps every edited file. It is well known that lexical and dense retrievers fail on different queries and that fusing them helps (Cormack et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2021). Our τ is the highest inverse document 1: canonical retrievals Dense (nDCG@10, advantage Figure over BM25 encoder jina-code-embeddings-0.5b, source-file labels) in the four Python pools, against three versions of BM25: untuned (the dense retrievers chunking, = 1,000), tuned (whole files), and tuned with LLM-written anchors added to the query (generate-then-grep). Tuning BM25 shrinks the premium to +0.03+0.13; adding anchors removes it in every pool, with BM25 significantly ahead on the curated pool. Means with repository-clustered 95% CIs  (Table 2)  . test pool  (Table 1)  . The two preregistered tests are scored on the labels as released (edited tests included), with source-file results alongside. We use grep for lexical search and measure it with ranked BM25, so generate-then-grep is BM25 on an expanded query; only the agent evaluation (Section 5.7) lets agents call grep directly on 96 tasks. We call dense retrievals nDCG@10 lead over BM25 the dense premium and ask three questions. How large is it under one consistent protocol? Which queries carry it? Should system route each query to retriever or fix one setup? Hybrid retrieval is known to help (Thakur et al., 2021), and LLM query expansion helps both BM25 and dense retrieval (Wang et al., 2023a; Gao et al., 2023). We use them as controlled interventions, asking which retriever expansion helps and why, and test our advice on preregistered held-out repositories. We evaluate thirteen dense encoders, plus SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021) and ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022). Our experiments identify where the premium comes from: F1 Evaluation choices inflate the dense advantage; smaller lead survives on raw queries. Indexing whole files for BM25 cuts the curated premium from +0.121 to +0.034; counting edited tests as relevant doubles the RAW-POST premium 2 frequency (IDF) among tokens shared by the query and the first source file the change edited. We compute IDF over the repositorys chunks. It adapts the MaxIDF predictor (Hauff et al., 2008) but needs the gold file; its proxy (cid:98)τ uses the query alone. LLM query expansion helps BM25 (Wang et al., 2023a) and, through generated pseudo-documents, dense retrieval (Gao et al., 2023). We use it as controlled intervention, not as proposed method. The closest work, SWE-Explore (Zhang et al., 2026a), also isolates retrieval: it scores the code regions that successful agents read, under line budget, and its dense baseline uses static word embeddings. We score the files the change edited, use current code encoders, and vary the lexical baseline, the label rule and the query source. Section gives further references.

sections.title: 3 REPOPREMIUM Construction
sections.content: 3.1 Task and Data Task. REPOPREMIUM is file retrieval inside one repository. Input: natural-language description of code change (an issue statement or PRs title and body) and pinned snapshot of its repository. Output: ranking of the snapshots files. Relevant: the non-test source files the described change edited. Test files stay in the ranking but count as non-relevant, and every retriever ranks the same files for the same query (an example in Figure 2). Two sets: REPOPREMIUM-CORE and REPOPREMIUM-EXT. The data has two sets  (Table 1)  . REPOPREMIUM-CORE carries the main results. Its four query pools differ in how the query was written and when the change was made, but share ten Python repositories, one code snapshot per repository (except RAW-PRE23, Step 6) and one label rule. The pools are curated statements from before the encoders cutoffs (CUR-PRE) and raw PR text from three windows: after the cutoffs (RAW-POST), 2023 (RAW-PRE23) and 2022 (RAW-PRE22). Because the code is shared, differences between pools come from the queries. The pools still describe different changes, so these comparisons are descriptive. The core is Python-only because SWE-bench Verified, the source of the curated queries, is Python-only, and the raw pools must use the same repositories. REPOPREMIUM-EXT checks whether the core results hold elsewhere. Each pool uses its own repositories. The curated rewrite states the behavior in the codes terms, and BM25 ranks the gold file first. In the raw PR title, the words DOC and docs (highlighted) pull BM25 toward documentation files, while dense retrieval still ranks the gold file first. Gold sets are the source files the change edited (Step 3). Multi-SWE-bench statements outside Python; nine held-out Python repositories; and DeepSWE tasks written by benchmark authors. matched replication also presents each of 360 changes twice, as the raw PR and as an LLM rewrite, so only the wording changes. All pools use the same label rule, and their raw PR text goes through the same filters and stripper. DeepSWE and the TypeScript, Go and Rust PRs form the preregistered lockbox, on which we tested routing and fusion once. holds 1,265 Scale. REPOPREMIUM-CORE queries over 10,200 indexed files (from 35 to 2,752 per repository; Table 6). REPOPREMIUMEXT adds 1,560 queries, counting both views of each matched task, from five more languages (JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java), nine held-out Python repositories and 88 DeepSWE repositories  (Table 1)  . Why rank whole files, not functions or lines? Repository-level work starts by choosing which files to edit: an engineer or an agent opens few files and edits within them. Localization pipelines rank files before functions or lines (Xia et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025). SWE-benchs retrieval baseline ranks whole files with BM25 (Jimenez et al., 2024). Bug localization has long ranked files against bug reports (Zhou et al., 2012). Finer-grained work ranks functions or line regions (Reddy et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). File labels also come straight from the merged change, so no annotator judges Figure 3: Construction pipeline of the four REPOPREMIUM-CORE pools (Steps 16 of Section 3.2); the REPOPREMIUM-EXT pools of Table 1 reuse Steps 35 on their own repositories. Curated SWE-bench Verified statements (blue) and raw merged-PR text (orange) share the label rules, preprocessing and one code snapshot per repository (RAW-PRE23 uses 2024-Q1 snapshot). Text filters apply to raw PRs only. Of 2,733 candidates, 1,265 remain in the four core pools. relevance. Scoring is still fine-grained: the encoder embeds 1,000-character chunks, and file takes its best chunks score. The task is not easy either: repositories hold up to 2,752 files, and no pipeline we ran exceeds 0.7 nDCG@10. 3.2 Construction Pipeline Six steps build the REPOPREMIUM-CORE pools (Figure 3). The REPOPREMIUM-EXT pools reuse the label rule and, for raw PR text, the filters and stripper (Steps 35), but index their own repositories; the appendix details each pool and its results. Step 1: Repositories. The core uses ten of the twelve SWE-bench Verified repositories; the other two have too few merged PRs. RAW-POST covers nine, as sphinx merged too few in 2026. Step 2: Queries. CUR-PRE takes each SWEbench Verified issue statement. The raw pools take the title and body of merged PRs from each date window, most recent first (up to 100 per repository, 40 for RAW-PRE23). Step 3: Gold labels. The gold set is the indexed source files the change edited, each with binary relevance. CUR-PRE reads them from the SWEbench gold patch, which has no tests. For raw PRs we drop edited tests and unindexed files (documentation, changelogs) from the changed-file list, matching SWE-benchs oracle files. Because this choice moves the premium, we also score with tests included (Section B.3). Step 4: Quality filter. query is kept if it has one to three gold files and every one exists at the snapshot; change that creates its source file is dropped rather than relabeled. Raw PRs must also describe code change (at least 100 characters, at most 20 edited files, not docs-, CIor test-only). Of 2,733 candidates, 1,265 remain  (Table 5)  : changes that edit few existing source files. Step 5: Preprocessing. regex stripper removes PR templates, checklists and HTML comments that otherwise swamp BM25 (Sections D.1 and J). Step 6: Corpus. Each repository is pinned at the base commit of its most recent SWE-bench Verified instance, and every .py file is one document; RAW-PRE23 uses 2024-Q1 snapshot. RAWPOSTs queries and changes therefore postdate the encoders, but the indexed code does not. Rescoring each task at its own base commit moves no tuned premium by more than 0.025 (Section B.2). Further construction details are in Section B. Release. We release the queries, file-level labels with test-file flag, pinned commits, the stripper and all evaluation harnesses (Section G).

sections.title: 5 Results and Analysis
sections.content: 5.1 How Large Is the Premium? Chunking decides the sign; whole-file BM25 removes most of the gap. On django, dense retrieval over whole files loses to BM25 ( = 0.153) because the encoders truncate long files; chunking at = 1,000 flips this to +0.119. BM25, in contrast, gains from larger windows. Against whole-file BM25 the premium falls to +0.034 on CUR-PRE and +0.059 to +0.125 on the raw pools  (Table 2)  . No encoder keeps significant premium on CUR-PRE or RAW-POST, and seven of thirteen fall significantly below zero on CUR-PRE (Ta5 ble 15). BM25s setting was picked on the evaluation queries, so these are lower bounds for dense retrieval. Counting test files as relevant inflates the premium. Dense retrievers rank test file first far more often than BM25 (59% against 34% of curated queries). Adding edited tests to the gold sets therefore raises the tuned premium from +0.034 to +0.165 on CUR-PRE and from +0.059 to +0.136 on RAW-POST (Section B.3). With either rule applied to every pool, the curated and raw pools are indistinguishable. Mixing the rules, as happens when SWE-bench gold patches are scored next to PR file lists, widens the RAW-POST-minus-CURPRE gap from +0.025 to +0.102. What survives is mostly coverage. Dense retrieval places more gold files in its top 10 (Recall@10 +0.10 to +0.19) but ranks its first hit significantly higher only on RAW-PRE22  (Table 11)  . Outside Python, modest premium remains on TypeScript and Rust but not on Go (single repositories; Section B.6). Much of the reported premium thus comes from the setup. Against whole-file BM25 the curated premium nearly vanishes (+0.121 +0.034), and the raw premiums shrink by third to over half. Counting test files as relevant inflates it again. What survives is mostly wider coverage. 5.2 Supplying the Missing Evidence If the premium reflects lexical evidence query lacks, supplying that evidence should help BM25 more than dense retrieval. Raw wording raises the premium within task. 36-repository replication pairs each raw PR with an LLM rewrite of the same change, against one gold set and corpus. With the LLM fixed, SWE-agent on the held-out pool (96 tasks) scores within about 0.04 exact-match whether it gets an unrestricted shell with grep, lexical index, dense index or (cid:98)τ -router. For agents, then, the choice of LLM matters far more for localization than the search tool it calls.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: Reconciling the debate. Benchmark gaps and agent experience can both be right. Against BM25 with the dense retrievers chunking, or with edited tests counted as relevant, dense encoders lead by 0.10.2 nDCG@10. Against whole-file BM25 on source-file labels they lead by little, mostly in coverage. Where they still lead, the query names no rare identifier. language model can add those identifiers, and grep-style search then matches the encoder. An agent that picks its own search terms does the same. Fusing the two retrievers still beats either alone  (Table 3)  . 5.6 Predicting the Winning Retriever The headroom is real. BM25 strictly beats dense retrieval on 24% of CUR-PRE and 21% of RAWPOST queries, and per-query oracle would add about 0.09 nDCG@10 over dense alone. No classifier or LLM judge we tried finds those queries. We tried classifiers on structural query features, logistic regression on query embeddings and two zero-shot LLM judges (qwen35-122B, gemma-4-31B-it). All reach AUROC 0.470.54, with every interval covering 0.5  (Table 19)  . Once Guidelines. G1 Measure dense gains against fair lexical baseline: whole files for BM25, templated PR text stripped, and one stated rule for which edited files count as relevant, applied to every query source. Report Recall@10 and an anchoraugmented BM25 arm next to the dense number. G2 Keep dense retrieval and fuse it with whole-file BM25; per-query routing did not beat the fusion. If the caller is an agent, spend on the model before the search endpoint. G3 When query lacks the codes vocabulary, add LLM-written anchors before searching. The call recurs per query, so dense index is cheaper for repositories searched often (Section E). We release REPOPREMIUM with source and test labels, the PR-boilerplate stripper, and the generation and agent-evaluation harnesses.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The core covers ten Python repositories and the cross-language PR pools one repository per language, so modest effects cannot be excluded. BM25 was tuned on the evaluation queries, generation results depend on the generator, and labels are the files one change edited. Functionand linelevel targets are untested.

sections.title: A Extended Related Work
sections.content: Benchmarks. Agent suites refresh or harden SWE-bench (Zhang et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Merrill et al., 2026) but score the whole agent loop, so they cannot attribute failure to retrieval. Code-retrieval benchmarks (Husain et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2026a) use docstring, web or competition queries rather than repository changes. SWE-Explore (Zhang et al., 2026a) labels the line regions that successful agents read. Its explanation of why lexical search fails on issue text matches what τ measures: the issue names no rare identifier of the edited module. Our encoders descend from code pretraining (Feng et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021, 2022; Wang et al., 2023b); the canonical one is jina-code (Kryvosheieva et al., 2025). dense, Retrieval methods. Fusion, lateinteraction, learned-sparse and cascaded pipelines combine lexical and dense signals (Cormack et al., 2009; Karpukhin et al., 2020; Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022; Formal et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021; Lin and Ma, 2021; Campese et al., 2024); we ask when the dense signal adds value and whether that can be predicted per query. τ builds on pre-retrieval query-performance prediction (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002; He and Ounis, 2004; Hauff et al., 2008; Carmel and Yom-Tov, 2010; Zhou and Croft, 2007; Arabzadeh et al., 2021). LLM query expansion helps BM25 and dense retrieval (Jagerman et al., 2023; Mackie et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Gao et al., 2023); we use it as controlled intervention against pseudo-relevance feedback (Lavrenko and Croft, 2001). LLM systems outside code also rewrite user request into search queries before retrieving, for example over knowledge base and web search engine (Xue et al., 2023). Rerankers trained on general web data transfer imperfectly to new domains (Xue et al., 2026b); our reranker baseline (jina-reranker-v3) is such general-purpose model. Embeddings beyond code. survey of omnimodal embeddings (Zhang et al., 2026b) organizes cross-modal unification around coverage, comparability and compositionality. Domain-specific retrieval also requires careful evaluation: ZooClawFashionSigLIP2 (Xue and Xu, 2026) studies adaptation to fashion retrieval and structural biases in benchmark ground truth. These broader settings motivate examining how benchmark construction shapes measured retrieval gains; our experiments isolate this question for repository code search. Practice and contamination. The claim we test is that embeddings were not the bottleneck for grep-driven SWE-bench agent (Chen and Flaherty, 2025); code-graph systems argue for structural retrieval instead (Abdelaziz et al., 2021). Contamination work (Magar and Schwartz, 2022; Sainz et al., 2023) motivates our post-cutoff pools and the exposure test of generation.

sections.title: B Benchmark Construction Details
sections.content: The construction keeps the pools comparable. Every pool uses one corpus snapshot per repository and one label rule (the indexed, non-test files change edited), and every raw pool uses the same text filters. The checks below show that the snapshot, unlabeled relevant files and BM25s tokenizer do not drive the results, but the test-file rule does. B.1 Construction Details by Step These notes add to Steps 16 of Section 3.2 only what the main text omits. Repositories. SWE-bench Verifieds 500 instances cover twelve repositories; seaborn and flask are too small for raw pools, leaving ten with enough merged PRs in every window. The core is Python because SWE-bench Verified is; Multi-SWE-bench enters as an REPOPREMIUMEXT pool (Section L), since its Python split repackages SWE-bench Verified. Mining and labels. Raw PRs come from the GitHub search API, most recent first, capped at 100 per repository (40 for RAW-PRE23); the query is the PR title and body. Gold files come from the SWE-bench gold patch (CUR-PRE) or the PRs changed-file list (raw pools). The gold patch has no tests. PR file lists, by contrast, include tests, documentation, changelogs and configuration files, so scored gold sets keep only indexed, non-test files (Section B.3). The release flags each edited file as source, test or non-indexed. In the raw pools, tests are 2933% of edited files and appear in 5863% of queries. Unindexed documentation, changelogs and templates are 2932% and appear in about half of queries. RAW-PRE22 was added because RAW-PRE23, mined at 40 PRs per repository, is small. Filtering. Filters apply in the order of Table 5. The gold rule asks for one to three scored gold files, all present at the snapshot, so changes that add their source file are excluded. Edited tests and documentation do not count toward the cap and need not exist. The cap keeps the task localization problem. The text rule drops bodies under 100 characters, PRs touching more than 20 files and docs-, CIor test-only changes. Paths under src/X map to when only the latter exists. Analyses that needed new retrieval runs use the 461 raw queries of the original, stricter rule. The queries added by the unified rule have lower premium at = 1,000, but no detectable difference in the tuned premium or the generation comparison. sphinx yields no RAW-POST query: it merged ten PRs in the 2026 window. Preprocessing. Raw PR descriptions carry ticket headers, checklists, AI-disclosure sections, checkbox lines and HTML comments; unstripped, BM25 on django RAW-POST collapses to nDCG@10= 0.010. The stripper (Section J) shortens raw queries by about 40% and curated statements by about 4%. Corpus. Each repository is pinned at the base commit of its most recent SWE-bench Verified instance, so every CUR-PRE base commit precedes the snapshot. The corpus is every .py file, tests included  (Table 6)  . RAW-PRE23 uses 2024-Q1 snapshot. As result, most curated fixes are already in the snapshot, and the RAW-POST changes come about three years after the indexed code. Post-cutoff therefore describes the query and the change but not the code. Section B.2 tests whether this matters. B.2 Per-Task Pre-Change Snapshots The shared snapshot does not drive the premium. We re-score 933 core queries at each tasks own base commit (834 commits). Retrieval is otherwise identical, and guard reproduces the sharedsnapshot results exactly. No tuned premium moves by more than 0.025, and the raw-minus-curated gap is unchanged  (Table 7)  . The curated premium rises slightly, so snapshot that already contains the fix favors BM25 little on curated queries. B.3 Label Definition and the Test-File Bias Counting edited test files as relevant rewards habit of dense retrievers, not localization. If one rule is used for all pools, either source files only or all edited files, the curated and raw premiums are indistinguishable. Only mixing the two separates them  (Table 8)  . Rule. file is test if its path contains test directory (test, tests, testing, __tests__, . . . ) or its name matches test pattern (test_*.py, conftest.py, *_test.go, *.spec.ts, . . . ); it is indexed if the pools corpus indexes its extension. Every analysis is re-scored from stored top-10 lists with these files removed from the gold set; retrieved tests then count as non-relevant. Dense retrievers rank tests first far more often. Dense retrieval puts test file first for 59% of curated and 2835% of raw queries, against 34% and 1216% for tuned BM25. Word overlap and file names do not explain this: those tests share fewer query words than the source files dense retrieval ranks, and few are named after gold module. Reproduction code in the query strengthens the preference, but it remains when the query has no code. Beyond code. Many relevance labels are harvested from records made for other purposes, such as changes file list, tickets links or clinical notes codes. The harvesting rule then decides what counts as relevant, and retriever families may differ in how easily they find the extra items. retrieval comparison is only as consistent as its label rule. B.4 Audit of Unlabeled Retrieved Files Missing labels lower both retrievers scores about equally, so they do not explain the premium. An LLM judge (qwen35-122B) read each change description together with the top-3 non-gold files from the canonical encoder and from whole-file BM25. One gold file per query was mixed in without its label. We used all 132 original RAW-POST queries and 132 sampled CUR-PRE queries. The judge marked 7578% of gold files as files to edit, but only 56% of the non-test misses, with no difference between the retrievers. sections.title: D Extended Findings
sections.content: Three results support the main text. BM25 is usable on raw text only after PR templates are stripped. The τ -effect is weak per query but large across query groups, and it is exploratory. Under one label definition, the query pools are hard to tell apart. D.1 PR-Boilerplate Stripping Recovers BM25 Templates break BM25 but not dense retrieval, so queries taken from PRs or issues must be stripped. On raw RAW-POST queries stripping roughly halves the premium (+0.369 to +0.175), entirely 16 through BM25 gains. Without stripping, BM25 on django returns the same template-matching files (global_settings.py, docs/conf.py) for almost every query. The repeated headers, checklists and HTML comments dominate BM25s IDFweighted query, while the encoder largely ignores them. hand audit of eight stripped queries confirms that titles and substantive prose survive. D.2 The τ -Effect in Detail τ predicts how large the premium is for group of queries, not for single query, and the evidence for it is exploratory. τ is MaxIDF on the tokens query shares with τ (q) (equation (1)) is the MaxIDF preits target. dictor of Hauff et al. (2008) restricted to tokens shared with the first indexed, non-test gold file. We chose it among four variants because it transfers best across slices  (Table 13)  ; that choice was made on the same slices. Its query-only analogue (cid:98)τ carries little per-query signal. The premium falls with τ in both cells. Pooled quartile means fall monotonically, from +0.217 to +0.050; the raw cell decays more steeply, and the curated cell has one interior wobble. The association is weak per query but large per group. The τ quartile explains about 2% of perquery variance, as much as knowing the repository; most of that variance is metric noise. Yet the drop from the lowest to the highest quartile is as large as the whole spread of the premium across encoders. τ thus shows where the premium is but cannot route single queries (Section P). D.3 Query Source and Vintage in Detail Under one label rule the core pools are not distinguishable, vintage has no consistent effect, and the raw-PR premium recurs in other languages. The pooled curatedraw gap was mostly label contrast. With source-file labels the rawminus-curated gap is +0.031 and not significant under repository-block resampling; keeping the raw pools edited tests more than doubles it (Section B.3). The pools also differ in repositories, query length and gold-set size, so even the residual gap is descriptive. Wording does matter when the task is held fixed (Section O). Vintage has no consistent effect. On 11 further Python repositories, we score PRs from 2022 and from 2026 against one pinned snapshot per repository. The date contrast has both signs across repositories and pools; pooled, it is +0.019. Contamination would predict smaller post-cutoff premium, which we do not see, though modest effect is not excluded. The raw-PR premium recurs outside Python. At = 1,000 raw PRs keep premium in JavaScript, TypeScript, Go and Rust; against the strongest BM25 we ran it remains on TypeScript and Rust but not on Go (Section B.6). Each language is single repository.

sections.content: (Exploratory) Across 38 evaluation slices the premium falls with τ in all but one, and one common slope fits them. Because the predictor and its normalization were chosen on these slices, this is exploratory; preregistered test on held-out repositories had the predicted sign but missed its criterion. Model and slices. We fit the premium as one common function of τ within-repository percentile (IDF is not comparable across corpora) plus per-slice offset. The slices cover the five Python mining regimes, all thirteen encoders on CUR-PRE and RAW-POST, the held-out pool and four other languages (9,339 queryslice observations). One slope fits all slices. The per-slice slope is negative in 37 of 38 slices. Encoders sharing pool are not independent, so the fairer count is nine of ten distinct query pools; the exception, RAW-PRE23, is small and near zero. The common slope is 0.165 nDCG@10 across the full percentile range; intervals resample repositories, then tasks, so encoders sharing task move together. Dropping any one repository barely changes the slope. homogeneity test does not reject single slope. Per-slice slopes are noisy, so we make the claim for the pooled data only (Figure 5). The preregistered held-out test was not met. We applied the frozen predictor to the 29 repositories of the matched replication (Section O) that no slice used. The slope is negative in all seven subslices (0.109 pooled), but its interval includes zero. With about ten tasks per repository, the within-repository percentile is too coarse to resolve slope of this size. sections.title: O A Matched Replication at Scale
sections.content: Holding the change fixed, raw PR wording raises the premium over curated rewrite of the same change, for two encoders from different families. date effect of similar size cannot be excluded, and the curated premium itself depends on the encoder. Design. We mine 360 PRs from 36 repositories in Go, Java, Python, Rust and TypeScript/JavaScript, five before and five after the encoders cutoffs per repository; 351 keep an indexed, non-test gold file and are scored. Each task is queried twice, against one gold set and one corpus at its base commit: once with the raw PR text and once with curated rewrite. qwen35-122B wrote the rewrite from the PR text without seeing gold paths or patches, and separate call to the same model checked its fidelity. The curated view is thus an LLM rewrite, not human curation. repository-disjoint development/test split was frozen before analysis. Wording moves the premium within task. Raw wording raises the premium for both jina-code-0.5b and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, in about 70% of repositories and on the held-out test split  (Table 18)  . Both views share one gold set, so the label rule cannot create this contrast. This is our strongest evidence that wording moves the premium; the pooled ten-repository comparison no longer separates curated from raw pools once labels are consistent (Section D.3). Only the raw premium survives change of encoder. The canonical encoder keeps premium on both views, but the second encoders curated premium is indistinguishable from zero, as it is on never-mined DeepSWE descriptions (Section R). This is what we expect if the premium is property of the query. Date is not separated from wording. The postminus-pre contrast points the way contamination predicts and is about half the size of the wording effect. Its interval includes zero, and direct comparison of the two sizes does not separate them. By language, all ten estimates point the same way, but only Python (and, for the second encoder, TypeScript/JavaScript and Rust) excludes zero on its own. We therefore do not claim five-language replication. When BM25 Wins BM25 wins sizable minority of queries, but nothing we tried could tell which ones from the query, so none of the predictors we tested could use this headroom. The headroom is real. BM25 strictly beats dense retrieval on about quarter of CUR-PRE and fifth of RAW-POST queries, and picking the better list per query would add about 0.09 nDCG@10 over dense alone. We tried classifiers on seven structural query features (with or without (cid:98)τ and length), classifier on the querys embedding, and two zero-shot LLM judges. Under leave-one-repository-out evaluation, none predicts BM25 wins better than chance. Tuned on the training repositories, each falls back to (nearly) always choosing dense  (Table 19)  . Untuned, the judges pick keyword search for most queries and lose over 0.1 nDCG@10. Even τ , which uses the gold file, separates BM25 wins only weakly. The RAW-POST sample is small, so modest signal on raw queries cannot be excluded. Agent-Driven End-to-End Evaluation Retrieval quality does not decide agent localization. For SWE-agent on the held-out pool, the choice of LLM moves exact-match far more than the choice of search tool. Our first version of this evaluation was invalid because the merged fix was reachable through git; all numbers here come from the clean rerun. Setup. We draw stratified samples from the heldout pool (Section B.7), balanced across its nine repositories: 30 queries for the model comparison and nesting draw of 96 for the search-tool comparison. The agent is mini-swe-agent (Princeton NLP, 2025) in its raw-shell configuration (temperature 0, 30 steps, 900 per query). It sees the raw problem statement and is scored on the files its final diff touches against the gold files: precision, recall, any-hit (at least one gold file) and exact-match (the gold set exactly). The model matters most. Across four openweight configurations  (Table 20)  , exact-match ranges from 0.033 (gemma-4-31B-it) to 0.300 (kimi-k3). Turning off qwen35-122Bs reasoning phase changes exact-match by an amount we cannot resolve, so the data do not show that thinking helps. The spread across families mixes family with scale: it shows that the served model matters, but not why. Low-recall trajectories share one failure: the agent commits to wrong file early and keeps editing it. Q.1 Search Tools at Fixed LLM At fixed LLM the search tool barely matters: four very different tools land within about 0.04 exactmatch of each other, and no difference between them is resolved. Design. We fix the LLM (qwen35-122B, thinking on) and replace the shells search with one tool, repo_search. Its backend is BM25, the canonical dense encoder, or router that uses (cid:98)τ to pick one of the two per query. The restriction is enforced: find, grep, rg and git grep are shadowed on PATH, and attempts around them are logged. No tool wins. The no-think column runs the same weights with the reasoning phase disabled; kimi-k3 replaces the withdrawn kimi-k2.6 of the superseded run and is reported in thinking mode only. Limitations. The model comparison uses 30 queries, so only its largest differences resolve. Scoring is file-level: any-hit is lenient ceiling and no execution-based check is run. The search tools return 20 chunk hits that are not deduplicated to files. Never-Mined Queries (DeepSWE) DeepSWE task descriptions are written to specify work, not mined from completed change. On them the premium does not transfer and BM25 wins far more often, which fits the view that the premium depends on how queries are written. Setup. 109 of DeepSWEs 113 tasks pass our qrel audit (88 repositories, five languages: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go and Rust). The gold files are those of one reference patch, so we measure reference-edit localization rather than exhaustive relevance. The retrieval harness is that of Section 4. The premium does not transfer. The canonical encoders premium, +0.121 and +0.152 on our curated and raw pools, is not distinguishable from zero here, and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B falls below BM25  (Table 22)  . This is the sharpest limit on the premium we found, and it matches the within-task wording effect of Section O. Lexical rescue is property of the query. BM25 strictly wins 3852% of queries, against about fifth to quarter on our pools, and the two encoders BM25-win sets largely coincide. Corpus size does not explain it. If anything the premium shrinks as corpora grow, though no size tercile resolves. cludes zero. The ordering of the three tools also changes between the 30and 96-query samples  (Table 21)  . At 30 steps, what limits the agent is which file the LLM commits to, not how it found candidates. This does not show that agents write their own anchors; that argument rests on Section 5.2 and Section R. The τ -effect reaches the agent on any-hit only. preregistered test predicted that the dense tool beats the BM25 tool on queries with few rare anchors (bottom (cid:98)τ quartile) and not on the top quartile. On any-hit it holds: dense is well ahead at the bottom and behind at the top, so the flat pooled comparison hides large swing. On exact-match the contrast is unresolved: finding some gold file more often does not mean reproducing the whole gold set. Q.2 Task-Environment Contamination Our first version of this evaluation leaked the answer, and the leak reversed its main result. We report it because the mistake is easy to make in any benchmark built from merged changes. What went wrong. Tasks were materialized with git worktree add at the base commit. This pins the files but shares the object store, so the merged fix stayed reachable through git log --all or git show. In 8 of 30 shell trajectories the agent read later commit covering the whole gold set. The tool restriction was also only request in the prompt, which the agent ignored in most trajectories. The fix, and what it changed. Each task is now exported with git archive into fresh repository with one synthetic commit and no remotes, checked per query. The tool restriction is enforced, and the shell has no network access; this also closes the route by which one query had fetched its own pullrequest diff. Raw-shell exact-match fell from 0.333 to 0.133, while the BM25 tool, which had nothing to gain from the leak, stayed at 0.167.
